moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
learningObjectives: Use Conditions to make a step or loop run only when a specific runtime state is true.
Use Parameters to pass variable data into steps and groups instead of hardcoding values.
Use Wait For to make a step wait on a specific condition before proceeding, instead of a fixed delay.
Search within a test to quickly locate a step, and recover an interrupted, unsaved test session.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Conditions: running steps only when it makes sense

elements.description: Conditions can be applied to a step (run it or not) or to a loop (repeat it or not). If a condition is false, the default behavior is to skip the step immediately or end the loop immediately; if true, the step executes or the loop repeats immediately.

Element conditions use visibility; Element text checks the selected target’s text; Custom permits JavaScript logic. Always Run and Never (skip) are additional execution choices. A condition gates execution, not an assertion that a business outcome occurred.

By default, a false condition immediately skips the step (or ends the loop). The 'retry' setting changes this: you specify a period in milliseconds during which Testim keeps re-checking the condition before giving up and moving on — useful for conditions tied to asynchronous UI states that need a moment to resolve.

elements.term: Setting a Custom condition on a step
elements.description: To attach a Custom (JavaScript) condition to a step or shared step: open the step, click the gear icon to open its Properties, find 'When to run step' (or 'When to run this step'), and select Custom — this opens the field where the JavaScript condition expression is written.

elements.title: A canonical Conditions use case
items: A Shared login group is called at the start of many tests.
Some of those tests already start in a logged-in session (e.g. persisted cookies); others don't.

A visibility condition can gate the shared login group. Independently establish the intended account/session state and assert the login outcome; a missing login button alone does not prove correct authentication.

bulletPoints: Conditions gate a step or a loop: false → skip/end immediately (by default); true → run/repeat immediately.
Element, Element text, and Custom (JS) are the core condition types.
Retry settings let a condition keep re-checking for a defined period instead of failing on the first false result.
Custom condition entry point: step's gear icon → Properties → 'When to run step' → Custom.
Gate optional login on inspected state, then assert the intended account and outcome.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Parameters: variable data instead of hardcoded values

elements.description: A parameter is a variable that can be used to pass information into a test step, letting the same step or group work with different data without needing separate, near-duplicate steps for each scenario.

Groups can define their own parameters. If a group is shared across multiple tests, those parameters remain available to every calling test — each test just sets its own values for the parameters rather than duplicating the group's underlying steps.

elements.text: Shared parameter definitions support reuse, with values supplied by each caller. Parameters must be used in supported fields; Variable Name, Description and Date Format are documented exceptions.

bulletPoints: Parameters = variables passed into a step so the same step handles multiple scenarios.
A shared group's parameters are available to every test that calls it — only the values differ per caller.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Generating dynamic test data: random values and dates

elements.description: Add Generate random value through predefined Actions. Configure character type, random length and optional prefix/suffix, then reference the stored variable in a later input. Randomness does not guarantee uniqueness; verify collision handling when uniqueness is required.

Add Generate date through predefined Actions. Configure the date format (default YYYY-MM-DD), signed offset and browser time or UTC. Match the application’s actual clock, timezone and required calendar semantics.

elements.title: A canonical Generate date use case
items: For an age-restricted registration example, derive representative dates relative to the intended reference clock.
Verify the produced date against the application’s age rule, timezone and leap-day policy.
Add explicit boundary cases on either side of the threshold; a single generated date is not maintenance-free proof of all age behavior.

bulletPoints: Generate random value and Generate date both live under the 'M' predefined steps menu → Actions.
Generate random value: String type + Length + optional Prefix/Suffix.
Generate date supplies relative values; validate clock, calendar and boundary expectations.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Finding your way around: search and draft recovery

elements.description: Within-test search is case-insensitive and requires at least three characters. It searches descriptions, code, parameters, supported URLs, data and conditions, but not every property. Documented exclusions include Sleep duration, Extract variable name and generated-value settings other than descriptions.

Testim stores a local recovery draft every 30 seconds. Recover restores the last available cached draft, so edits after that snapshot may be missing; cleared/unavailable cache cannot be treated as durable backup. Dismiss opens the last saved test. Save deliberately after recovery.

bulletPoints: Within-test search is case-insensitive and covers supported fields, with explicit exclusions.
Recover uses the last available local draft; Dismiss opens the saved test.
Always click Save after recovering — don't treat the auto-recovery draft as durable storage.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Wait For: condition-based waiting instead of fixed delays

elements.description: Condition-based waits retry until the required state is detected or the step timeout is reached. A condition that never becomes true must not hang indefinitely. Select a timeout and failure handling for the scenario.

elements.text: Condition-based synchronization can reduce unnecessary fixed delays, but polling and execution overhead mean it is not an exact-duration or no-flakiness guarantee. Sleep remains supported for deliberate fixed pauses.

bulletPoints: Wait for detected readiness with a bounded timeout.
A timeout or wrong readiness condition still requires diagnosis.

examPitfalls.title: Using a fixed-time delay instead of Wait For
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Adding an arbitrary pause (e.g. 'wait 5 seconds') to work around a slow-loading element.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Wait for the actual readiness condition with an appropriate timeout. This can reduce brittle fixed delays but does not guarantee faster execution or eliminate all timing failures.

examPitfalls.title: Duplicating steps instead of parameterizing them
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Creating near-identical copies of a group or test just to change one or two values (e.g. different usernames).
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Define Parameters on the group/step once, and let each calling test supply its own values — this keeps the underlying steps single-sourced and maintainable.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming a condition retries by default
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Expecting a condition tied to an async UI state to automatically wait and re-check before failing.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: By default, a false condition immediately skips the step or ends the loop. Explicitly enable the retry setting and specify a duration if the condition needs time to resolve.

examPitfalls.title: Hardcoding a fixed birthdate to test an age restriction
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Hardcoding a literal date like '2000-01-01' to represent 'a user who just turned 18', which silently drifts further from the boundary being tested as real time passes.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Generate representative relative dates and verify the application clock, timezone and calendar boundary policy. Maintain explicit before/at/after-threshold expectations instead of assuming a generated offset is permanently correct.

examPitfalls.title: Clicking Dismiss when you actually wanted the unsaved changes back
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Reopening a test after an interruption, clicking Dismiss out of habit, and losing edits that were sitting in the auto-saved draft.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Recover restores the last available cached snapshot; Dismiss opens the saved test. Save after recovery and do not assume every unsaved edit survived.

practiceQuiz.scenario: By default, what happens when a Condition attached to a step evaluates to false?

options.text: The entire test immediately fails.
The step is skipped immediately.
Testim retries the condition indefinitely until it passes.
The step runs anyway, ignoring the condition.

practiceQuiz.hint: The default behavior has no retry unless you configure one.
practiceQuiz.rationale: By default, if a condition for a step is false, the step is skipped immediately (a loop would end immediately). Retrying requires explicitly enabling the retry setting in Advanced Condition Settings.

optionExplanations.A: A false gate normally skips the step rather than failing the entire test.
optionExplanations.B: The default false-condition behavior is immediate skipping.
optionExplanations.C: Retries require explicit finite settings; they are not indefinite by default.
optionExplanations.D: The execution gate is not ignored.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A defined JavaScript parameter cart is available to the step. Which condition type supports evaluating cart.itemCount > 0 to gate execution?

options.text: Element
Element text
Custom
Wait For

practiceQuiz.hint: You need arbitrary logic, not just a presence or text check.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Custom condition type lets you write your own JavaScript expression for runtime logic that doesn't map to a simple element-presence or element-text check. Element and Element text are narrower, purpose-built condition types; Wait For is a separate mechanism for pausing, not a condition type.

optionExplanations.A: Element conditions check visibility, not arbitrary cart logic.
optionExplanations.B: Element text checks target text, not arbitrary cart state.
optionExplanations.C: Custom supports the defined JavaScript expression.
optionExplanations.D: Wait For is a synchronization step, not this condition type.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Shared Group implementing a login flow is called from 12 different tests, each with different credentials. How should the credentials be handled?

options.text: Create 12 near-identical copies of the group, one per test.
Define username/password as Parameters on the group, and have each calling test supply its own values.
Hardcode one set of credentials and require all 12 tests to use the same account.
Use Conditions instead of Parameters to select the credentials at runtime.

practiceQuiz.hint: This is exactly what Parameters on a shared group exist for.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Parameters on a shared group stay available to every calling test; each test just sets its own parameter values, keeping the underlying steps single-sourced instead of duplicated 12 times.

optionExplanations.A: Copies duplicate maintenance rather than share the logic.
optionExplanations.B: Each caller supplies credentials to one parameterized group.
optionExplanations.C: One hardcoded account does not implement differing credentials.
optionExplanations.D: An execution condition does not replace parameter inputs.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Why is a Wait For step generally preferred over a fixed-time delay before an asynchronous element appears?

options.text: Wait For steps run faster than any fixed delay, always.
It checks the readiness condition until detected or timeout, reducing dependence on a guessed fixed delay.
Fixed delays are not supported by Testim at all.
Wait For steps do not count toward the test's total run time.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's about matching the wait to the actual condition, not raw speed.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Condition-based waits synchronize with detected readiness up to the configured timeout. They do not guarantee exact timing, faster execution in every case or elimination of all failures; Sleep remains supported.

optionExplanations.A: Wait duration and success depend on actual readiness and timeout.
optionExplanations.B: Readiness polling can reduce dependence on a fixed guess and has a timeout.
optionExplanations.C: Sleep is supported for fixed pauses.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is a good scenario for when to use "Conditions" in Testim?

options.text: To run the same test steps on multiple browsers for cross-browser testing.
When you only want to run a log in shared step when a certain UI element is visible.
To generate and validate random data for input fields.
To debug test cases using the Testim CLI tool.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's the canonical login-group example: gate the step on whether login is actually needed.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Conditions are for gating whether a step runs — the classic case being a login shared step that should only execute when a specific UI element (like a login button) is actually visible. Cross-browser execution, random data generation, and CLI debugging are each handled by different, unrelated features.

optionExplanations.A: Browser configurations, not a visibility gate, define cross-browser coverage.
optionExplanations.B: A visibility gate can conditionally run a login group.
optionExplanations.C: Generation and assertions are different mechanisms.
optionExplanations.D: CLI debugging is not the purpose of an execution condition.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Where do you configure a Custom JavaScript execution condition on a shared step, rather than define test data?

options.text: Selecting predefined test data from the Testim dropdown menus.
Writing a SQL query within Testim to fetch test data from a database.
Going to the shared step and clicking the gear icon, select "When to run step" under Properties and select "Custom".
Select the gear icon and select Import JSON file in Testim.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's the same gear-icon → Properties → 'When to run step' path used to set any condition type.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A Custom JavaScript condition is set via the step's gear icon → Properties → 'When to run step' → Custom — the standard entry point for any condition type, not a dropdown of canned data, a direct SQL query, or a JSON import.

optionExplanations.A: A data dropdown does not configure Custom execution gating.
optionExplanations.B: Fetching database input is distinct from this condition setting.
optionExplanations.C: Properties > When to run step > Custom opens the execution condition configuration.
optionExplanations.D: JSON import does not configure the step gate.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Where can you find the "Generate Random Value" option in Testim when generating a random value?

options.text: Under Predefined steps > Actions > Generate random value
Under Shared steps > Actions > Generate random value.
Under the Test Editor's Step Properties
Under the Test Library > Generate random value

practiceQuiz.hint: It's a predefined step, added the same way as a validation or navigation step.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Generate random value is found under the predefined steps menu ('M' icon) → Actions → Generate random value — the same menu used to add other predefined action/validation steps, not something tied to Shared Steps, Step Properties, or the Test Library.

optionExplanations.A: Generate random value is a predefined Action.
optionExplanations.B: It is not added from the shared-group list.
optionExplanations.C: Properties configure an existing generator after insertion.
optionExplanations.D: The library is not the documented insertion menu.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which scenario specifically benefits from generated date input with verified reference-clock and boundary expectations?

options.text: When verifying the presence of a static image on a webpage.
Supplying relative birthdate inputs when checking an age restriction.
When debugging a test that fails due to incorrect element locators.
When testing whether a web page contains the correct error message for an invalid input field.

practiceQuiz.hint: It needs a date that stays correct relative to 'today', like a birthdate.
practiceQuiz.rationale: An age restriction needs date inputs and explicit expected boundary behavior. Verify the generated calendar date and clock policy; generation alone does not certify correctness indefinitely.

optionExplanations.A: Image presence does not require generated date input.
optionExplanations.B: Relative birthdates are relevant date inputs; assert the required boundaries.
optionExplanations.C: Date generation does not repair locators.
optionExplanations.D: A generic invalid-field message need not involve dates.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which statement about Search within a test (not Shared Steps Library search) is correct?

options.text: It is case sensitive.
It is not case sensitive.
It only searches for exact matches.
It searches only through JavaScript code.

practiceQuiz.hint: Also worth knowing: it scans far more than just step titles.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Search within a test is not case sensitive, and it scans a broad set of fields — step description, JS code, parameters, base URL, navigation/API URLs, test data, and conditions — not just JavaScript code, and not requiring exact-match text.

optionExplanations.B: The documented within-test search ignores case.
optionExplanations.C: It supports partial text matches with at least three characters.
optionExplanations.D: It searches supported fields beyond JavaScript code.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which of the following best explains the difference between the "Recover" and "Dismiss" options when recovering an unsaved test in Testim?

options.text: "Recover" restores the test to its last saved state, while "Dismiss" saves the unsaved draft.
Recover opens the last available cached draft; Dismiss opens the last explicitly saved test.
"Recover" opens a new draft of the test, while "Dismiss" deletes the test entirely.
"Recover" refreshes the page, while "Dismiss" keeps the page in its current state.

practiceQuiz.hint: One option resumes the draft; the other reverts to what was explicitly saved.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Recover uses the available locally cached draft, not necessarily the very latest edit. Dismiss opens the last saved test. Neither choice makes local draft caching a durable backup.

optionExplanations.B: Recovery uses the available draft; dismissal opens the saved test.
optionExplanations.C: Dismiss does not delete the entire saved test.
optionExplanations.D: The choices concern draft recovery, not merely page refresh.

quickRecap.value: Gate a step or loop on Element / Element text / Custom (JS) logic; false = skip/end immediately by default.
Makes a condition keep re-checking for a set duration instead of failing on the first false result.
Variables passed into a step/group so one set of steps serves many scenarios.
Stay available to every calling test — only the values differ per caller.
Checks readiness until detected or timeout; not an exact-duration or guaranteed-success wait.
Step's gear icon → Properties → 'When to run step' → Custom.
Both under the 'M' predefined steps menu → Actions; date supports a relative Time difference (e.g. for age-restriction testing).
Case-insensitive, minimum three characters; supported fields have documented exclusions.
Recover restores the available cached snapshot; Dismiss opens the saved test. Save after recovery.
